introduction: The Spanish SBA involves oral and written tasks that demonstrate language proficiency in a variety of contexts. It contributes to the final grade.

tasks.title: Written Component
tasks.explanation: A report or project based on a cultural theme or personal experience.

tasks.title: Oral Task
tasks.explanation: A conversation or presentation in Spanish.

tasks.title: Reflection
tasks.explanation: A reflection on the learning process.

sampleTitle: Una investigación sobre la importancia de la música en la cultura de México.

sample.body: México es un país con una rica tradición musical. Desde el Mariachi hasta la música pop moderna, el ritmo es parte de la vida diaria. Investigué esto leyendo sobre la historia de la música ranchera.
sample.tips: Use a variety of tenses (present, past) in your report.

sample.body: Para este proyecto, escuché muchas canciones mexicanas. Aprendí vocabulario nuevo y mejoré mi comprensión auditiva.
sample.tips: Speak clearly and focus on pronunciation during the oral phase.

marking: Grammatical accuracy, vocabulary range, and fluency in the oral component are the key areas for assessment.

completedSample.title: A complete Spanish dossier: the written task, the spoken talk and the reflection
completedSample.viewOnlyNote: For viewing and study only. This is an original dossier written for CSEC Compass by an invented candidate: the candidate, the school, the two listeners, the teacher's eight questions, the glossary and every count in it are invented, it is not a real candidate's work, not a record of a real examination, and not a CXC exemplar. Read it, study how the written task and the oral component were prepared, counted and repaired, then write and say your own answers about your own research.

categories.comment: Three drafts of the report on our guide's own topic (412, 547 and 667 words, with the per-section lengths in the table above), each draft read back and its faults counted (14, then 7, then 2), and a glossary of 40 terms tested three times (22, then 31, then 37). This is the 10 marks our guide lists for the written task.

The same research spoken in the report's own six sections, from cue cards and without reading: 468 words in 4 min 06 s, then 452 in 3 min 42 s, then 441 in 3 min 31 s, with the faults counted down from 30 to 16 to 5 and all eight of the teacher's questions answered in the final run. This is the 10 marks our guide lists for the oral component.

The reflection keeps the plan and the honest record of it: 25 of the 30 planned speaking sessions and 17 of the 20 planned writing sessions, 13 h 25 min of counted practice over ten weeks, with the two weeks that slipped named and the three habits the counts changed. This is the 5 marks our guide lists for the reflection.

pages.heading: Method - how this dossier was prepared, counted and repaired
pages.body: Ten weeks, forty-two sessions and seven recordings. The rule of the method was written into the plan on the first day: the topic belongs to our guide - the investigation it sets out is the investigation reported here - while the Spanish belongs to the candidate, and nothing is counted from memory. Every draft, every self-test and every recording was counted in the week it was made, which is why the counts that follow can be checked against one another.
bullets: 25 speaking sessions of five minutes and 17 writing sessions of forty minutes = 13 h 25 min of practice, against the 30 speaking and 20 writing sessions the plan asked for.
7 recordings kept, one in each week from week 4 to week 10; the last three are the whole talk, and the last two were counted by two listeners from the same tally sheet.
The glossary of 40 terms was tested three times, 22 then 31 then 37 correct, and every score was written down the same day - including the second one, taken in a week the plan had slipped.
The written task was read back three times and its faults counted: 14, then 7, then 2. The fair copy printed in this dossier is what came out of the last read.
The talk was rehearsed from six cue cards holding 127 key words in total and was delivered without reading; the words spoken were counted from the recordings, not estimated from the script.

pages.heading: Written Task - the report on the guide's own topic, section by section
pages.body:
The written task is the investigation our guide sets out - Una investigación sobre la importancia de la música en la cultura de México. - reported in Spanish and built over three drafts. The finished report is printed below in full, paragraph after paragraph: 667 words in 36 sentences, a mean of 18.5 words a sentence, and the longest paragraph of all, 74 words, is the one under the heading Conclusión. No sentence was added to reach a length: the two earlier drafts were shorter because there was less to say, not because the finished one was padded.

México es un país con una rica tradición musical. Desde el Mariachi hasta la música pop moderna, el ritmo es parte de la vida diaria. Investigué esto leyendo sobre la historia de la música ranchera.

Cuando la profesora nos pidió un tema cultural, pensé en la música porque está en todas partes: en la casa, en la calle y en las fiestas del pueblo. En México, una canción puede contar la historia de una familia o de una región entera. Para mí, la música es la manera más fácil de entender cómo vive la gente de otro país.

El mariachi es un grupo de músicos que toca en las bodas, en los cumpleaños y en las fiestas de la comunidad. Los instrumentos más comunes son la trompeta, el violín, la guitarra y la vihuela, y en algunas regiones se añade el acordeón. Los músicos llevan un traje con botones plateados y un sombrero grande, y todos cantan a la vez.

La música del mariachi empezó en el oeste de México y hoy se escucha en todo el país. En la investigación leí que el mariachi acompaña a la gente en los momentos importantes de la vida: cuando alguien se casa, cuando nace un niño y también cuando alguien muere. Por eso la música no es solo un espectáculo: es una compañía.

La música ranchera nació en el campo y habla del amor, del desamor y de la vida sencilla. Sus canciones son lentas y se cantan con la voz fuerte, casi como un grito, para que la letra llegue lejos. La ranchera cuenta lo que siente una persona: la nostalgia de la tierra, el dolor de una despedida o el orgullo de ser mexicano.

Muchas rancheras se acompañan con guitarra y trompeta, y algunas se cantan a caballo, en las fiestas del pueblo. Leí que la ranchera se hizo muy conocida cuando las películas mexicanas llevaron estas canciones a otros países de América Latina. En mi opinión, esa mezcla de sentimiento y sencillez es lo que mantiene viva la ranchera hoy.

Hoy la música mexicana moderna mezcla los ritmos tradicionales con el pop y el rock. Los grupos jóvenes usan la guitarra eléctrica, la batería y a veces también la trompeta, y cantan en español y en inglés. Muchas canciones hablan de la ciudad, del barrio y de la vida de los adolescentes, no solo del campo.

En la investigación vi que esta mezcla no borra la tradición: la letra sigue contando historias y el ritmo sigue invitando a bailar. Un ejemplo es el corrido moderno, que cuenta la vida de una persona o de un pueblo con un ritmo rápido.

En México la música acompaña casi todas las celebraciones. En una boda, el mariachi toca cuando llegan los novios y otra vez cuando la familia baila. Antes, la música se tocaba en la casa y en la plaza, y la gente bailaba en la calle. Hoy la fiesta también cabe en un altavoz.

En el Día de la Independencia, las bandas tocan en la plaza y la gente canta con la bandera en la mano. En diciembre, las posadas se hacen de casa en casa y siempre hay alguien con una guitarra. Escuché que en los desfiles también hay tamboras y trompetas. Para mí, esta es la parte más importante de la investigación: la música no se escucha solo en un concierto, se vive en el barrio.

Después de esta investigación, entiendo mejor por qué la música es tan importante en la cultura de México. No es solo un entretenimiento: guarda la memoria del pueblo, une a la familia y cambia con la gente que la escucha. El mariachi, la ranchera y el pop moderno son tres maneras de decir lo mismo: esto es lo que somos.

Aprendí que investigar un tema cultural también enseña vocabulario, y que una canción puede ser una fuente tan válida como un libro. Creo que la música mexicana seguirá cambiando, pero la fiesta será siempre un lugar para cantar juntos.

table.caption: The report, section by section. The two earlier columns are the lengths copied out of the week log (draft 1 and draft 2); the finished column and the share are counted from the text printed above, and the three columns add up to 412, 547 and 667 words.

pages.heading: Results - the glossary of forty words, tested three times
pages.body: Our guide's checklist asks for a vocabulary list, and this is where the list earned its keep: 40 terms, each one written on a card with the sentence it came from, and the same test taken three times - 22, then 31, then 37 correct out of 40. thirteen of the 40 were words that had not been met before, and the three still shaky in the last test are the three that had only ever been written down instead of said aloud. All three scores are kept, including the one taken after two weeks when the plan had slipped.

table.caption: The same forty terms, tested three times. Every score below is the number of terms that came out right, so the missed column and the score column add up to forty in every row.
columns: Of those, terms new to me
rows: end of week 6, after the two slipped weeks
end of week 9, the day before the first mock run

bullets: New words met during the research: thirteen. They are the reason the first score is the lowest.
Still shaky after the last test: la vihuela, el acordeón and la tambora.
Missed in the last test but already known before the research: none - every term still wrong in week 9 was a term met during the investigation.
The three self-tests are the whole evidence for the vocabulary claim: no score was estimated, and the terms that moved were moved by saying them, not by copying them.

pages.heading: Results - the eighteen terms missed first, and the card that settled each one
pages.body: 18 of the 40 terms were missed in the first test, and the table keeps them all, including the ones that were already known before the research and still came out wrong - a list that only holds its hard words is not a record of anything. Each row ends with the card that finally settled it, which is the only part of a glossary that a reader cannot guess.

table.caption: The first test's misses, kept in the order of the report. The card column is the fixed memory device written for each term, not a definition.
rows: the small guitar: the card shows it beside a full-size guitarra, so the two string words stay in one picture
the stress falls on the last syllable, a-cor-de-ON; the card was written out twice a week until the accent stopped moving
the big drum that carries a march: the card pairs tambora with tambor, which is the word for a drum
the ballad that tells a life: the card pairs corrido with contar, because both answer what it does
the song from the countryside: the card has campo on one side and ranchera on the other
the parade: the card walks the word across the page, one syllable a step, des-fi-le
the homeland: the card keeps patria and padre side by side, because both open with the same four letters
the neighbourhood: the card is the double rr, the same sound that was hardest to say in the talk
heritage: the card links herencia to heredar, which keeps the h and the first e in place
feeling: the card groups it with the other words built on -miento and underlines the ie
longing: three syllables with the stress on the middle one, nos-TAL-gia, and the card marks it
mixture: the card puts mezcla beside mezclar, so that the z stays a z
dance: the card pairs bailar (to dance) with baile (the dance), one letter apart
stage: split on the card as escena plus rio, because the stage is where the scene happens
memory: the card pairs memoria with recordar, a verb that appeared in every draft
the past: the card carries the report's own preterite sentence, so the tense and the word are learned together
community: the card keeps comunidad next to común, which is where the word starts
identity: the card keeps identidad next to idéntico, one ending apart

pages.heading: Results - the faults counted in each written draft, and how each group was closed
pages.body: 23 faults were found across the three drafts of the report: 14 in draft 1, 7 in draft 2 and 2 in the last read of draft 3, of which the fair copy printed in this dossier corrects one accent and one verb ending. The counts came from reading each draft back with a pencil, marking one fault at a time, and grouping them afterwards - which is why the groups can be followed from draft to draft.

table.caption: Every fault found in every draft, grouped by what it was, with the fix recorded beside it. The three columns sum to the fault totals above.
rows: Marked every verb in the draft with its tense before reading the rest of the sentence, instead of reading for meaning and hoping the ending was right.
Agreement of adjectives and nouns, singular or plural, masculine or feminine
Checked each adjective against its noun and wrote the pair on a card; the forms that look the same in writing were the ones that stayed wrong longest.
Accents written in or left out
Read every draft out loud, because a missing accent is nearly always a word that was being stressed in the wrong place when it was said.
Vocabulary choice - correct Spanish, but not the word a Mexican speaker would use
Replaced the dictionary word with the word from the source that had been read; one of these is still in the fair copy and was marked by the teacher's listener.
Closed in draft 2 and did not come back; the fix was to copy the whole phrase out of the source rather than the verb on its own.
The total fell by 12 between draft 1 and the last read

pages.heading: Results - the tense check: one sentence for each tense the report works in
pages.body: The tense check was the fix for the largest group of faults in draft 1, so it is kept here as the evidence for it. The report was read back with every verb marked, and the four tenses it works in are listed below with the sentence that shows each one; the reading was looking for a wrong ending or a missing accent inside a tense, not for a count of them.

table.caption: The tense check, one quoted sentence per tense. Every sentence below is a sentence of the report printed on the written-task page, quoted exactly.
columns: What it is doing in the report
rows: El mariachi es un grupo de músicos que toca en las bodas, en los cumpleaños y en las fiestas de la comunidad.
what the mariachi is and does today - the report describes a tradition that is still alive, so most of its verbs are in the present.
La música del mariachi empezó en el oeste de México y hoy se escucha en todo el país.
what happened and what was read: everything taken from a source is reported in the past, so a reader can tell the research from my own opinion.
Antes, la música se tocaba en la casa y en la plaza, y la gente bailaba en la calle.
how things used to be - the imperfect describes a habit rather than one evening, and it carries the comparison between then and now.
Creo que la música mexicana seguirá cambiando, pero la fiesta será siempre un lugar para cantar juntos.
what the tradition does next - the last paragraph looks forward, which is the only place in a piece of research where a future tense belongs.

pages.heading: Oral Component - the talk, its six sections and the cue card for each
pages.body: The oral component is the same research spoken rather than read: six sections in the order of the report, delivered from cue cards and recorded three times. The cards held 127 key words between them and the final run of the talk came to 441 words, which is the difference between a prompt and a script - the cue card for the mariachi section says trompeta, violín, guitarra, vihuela, and the sentence around those words is made up again every time it is spoken.

table.caption: The six sections of the talk in the order they were spoken, with the key words on each cue card. The words and the seconds are from the final mock run, and the seconds add up to its 3 min 31 s.
columns: Key words on the cue card
Words spoken in the final run

pages.heading: Results - the three recorded rehearsals, and the words a minute
pages.body: All three recordings were counted the same way, and the measures move together: the talk got shorter (468 words, then 452, then 441), faster (114, then 122, then 125 words a minute) and cleaner (30 faults, then 16, then 5). Nothing was recorded again to look better - the first recording is the first recording, hesitations and all, which is the only reason the last one can be trusted.

table.caption: The three recordings of the whole talk. The words a minute column is computed from the words and the seconds beside it, so the pace cannot be claimed without the recording to support it.

Counted by me, from the recording
week 9, in front of two listeners with the tally sheet
Two listeners, the same tally sheet
week 10, in front of two listeners with the tally sheet
Two listeners, the same tally sheet

bullets: The whole talk was there, but it was spoken to the desk and the hesitations were everywhere; the note kept with the recording says slow down, not speed up.
Faster and much clearer, but three of the teacher's eight questions produced a silence and the corrections were still audible.
Six sections in order, all eight questions answered, and the two faults left were both inside single words rather than in sentences.

pages.heading: Results - the thirty faults of the first rehearsal, grouped by what the examiner hears
pages.body: 30 faults were counted in the first rehearsal and 5 in the final mock run, and the grouping is what made the difference: the largest group was not pronunciation but hesitation, 11 of the 30 faults in the first rehearsal, and a hesitation cannot be heard from inside the sentence that carries it. The recording is the only reason that number exists.

table.caption: Every spoken fault counted across the three recordings, grouped by what the examiner hears rather than by what caused it. The columns sum to the fault totals in the rehearsal table on the previous page.
rows: A word pushed out with the English r or h instead of the Spanish rr or j
One line a day said out loud, then the same line played back and imitated; the two left in the final run were the stress of el acordeón and the rr of el barrio.
Hesitation markers - este, eh - inside a sentence
Counted every one of them from the recording and replaced it with a short pause; a second of silence sounds like thinking, and este sounds like a mistake.
Sentences started and then corrected out loud
Rehearsed the transition sentence between two sections, which is where every correction had happened, until it ran without a break.
Said the glossary aloud instead of reading it; the words that had only ever been written down were the ones that came out in English.
Learned one sentence for the end of every section, so that losing the thread would cost a sentence rather than a silence.
The total fell by 25 between the first recording and the last

pages.heading: Oral Component - the teacher's eight questions, and what was answered
pages.body: Our guide's oral component is a conversation as well as a presentation, so both mock runs ended with the same eight questions in the same order. four of the eight answers came out word for word from the four prepared answers, one was adapted from the glossary, and three were improvised on the day; the two that had produced a silence in week 9 are marked in the table.

table.caption: The eight questions of the final mock run, in the order they were asked, with the answer given and where it came from. The two improvised answers marked as silences are the two the first mock run could not produce.
columns: The answer given in the final run
rows: ¿Por qué elegiste la música como tema de tu investigación?
Elegí la música porque en México está en todas partes: en la familia, en la calle y en las fiestas.
prepared answer 1 (the topic), word for word
El mariachi es un grupo de músicos con trompetas y violines que toca en las bodas y en las celebraciones.
prepared answer 2 (the mariachi), word for word
¿Cuál es la diferencia entre la música ranchera y el pop moderno?
La ranchera habla del amor y del campo, y el pop moderno mezcla los ritmos mexicanos con el inglés.
improvised - this question produced the first silence in week 9
¿En qué fiestas se escucha la música mexicana?
En las bodas, en el Día de la Independencia y en las posadas de diciembre.
prepared answer 3 (the celebrations), word for word
¿Qué instrumentos aparecen en la música mexicana?
La guitarra, la trompeta, el violín y la vihuela; en el norte también el acordeón.
adapted from the glossary - the same list, said as a list rather than written down
El acordeón: siempre lo decía con el acento en la sílaba equivocada.
improvised - this question produced the second silence in week 9
Grabé la presentación tres veces y conté los errores; en la última solo quedaron cinco.
prepared answer 4 (the method), word for word
¿Crees que la música es importante en la cultura de México?
Sí: une a la familia y al barrio, y guarda la memoria del país.
improvised - an opinion with one reason, which the guide's own method asks for

bullets: Prepared answer 1 - why I chose music: it is everywhere in Mexico, in the family, in the street and at the celebrations.
Prepared answer 2 - what the mariachi is: a group of musicians with trumpets and violins who play at weddings and celebrations.
Prepared answer 3 - the celebrations: weddings, Independence Day and the December posadas.
Prepared answer 4 - how I improved: three recordings of the whole talk, with the faults counted each time.

pages.heading: Results - the two mock runs, counted the same way
pages.body: Both mock runs were counted by two listeners, with the same tally sheet, in weeks 9 and 10. Every measure improved except the time spent on the talk itself, which was the one thing that did not need to change: 8 of the 8 questions were answered in the final run against 5 in the first, the glossary words used inside the talk went from 12 of 40 to 19, and the seconds lost to pauses went from 18 to none.

table.caption: The same tally sheet for both mock runs. Every row is a count, and the fault rows are a breakdown of the fault total rather than a second count of it.
rows: Seconds lost to pauses over five seconds
The teacher's questions answered, of eight
Answers carrying a reason or an extra detail
Glossary words used in the talk, of forty

pages.heading: Discussion - what the counts exposed, and the three habits I changed
pages.body: If the counts say one thing, it is that the Spanish was rarely the problem and the preparation often was. The first rehearsal carried 30 faults and 11 of them were hesitation markers - the biggest single group, and the one I could not hear while speaking, because inside the talk every este felt like thinking. The two silences of the first mock run were both questions rather than sections, which is why the questions now have their own page in the plan instead of being left to the morning of the run.
bullets: Change 1: record the talk and count the faults instead of repeating it, because the faults that embarrass a speaker (11 hesitation markers in the first rehearsal) are exactly the faults a speaker cannot hear.

Change 2: prepare an answer for every question as well as for every section. The two silences of the first mock run were the only two questions that had not been written out, and both are answered in the table above.

Change 3: say the new words out loud inside the talk, not only in the report. The glossary words used while speaking went from 12 of 40 to 19, and the three words left shaky after three written tests are the three that had never been spoken.

Kept honestly: the thirty faults of the first rehearsal, the 3 English words that slipped into it, the three questions left unanswered in week 9, and the two weeks (weeks six and seven) that lost most of their sessions.

pages.heading: Strategy - my reflection on the learning process, week by week
pages.body:
The reflection is the smallest task in our guide's breakdown (5 of the 25 marks it lists) and it is the one that changed how the other two were done. The plan was 30 speaking sessions of five minutes and 20 writing sessions of forty minutes over ten weeks; the table is what actually happened, week by week, including the two weeks the plan lost and what was done about them.

The lesson I would keep: a session missed is not a session lost if the next one starts where the last one stopped. Weeks 6 and 7 took the concert and the end-of-term tests, and the report still finished on time because the glossary was tested in week 9 rather than read again.

pages.heading: Conclusion - what this dossier shows, and what not to copy from it
pages.body:
The oral component is marked on how the candidate speaks and the written task on what the candidate writes, and nothing in this dossier would survive being copied: the talk is six sections of one student's own research and the eight questions follow that research. What a reader can take from it is the method, not the words - three drafts with their faults counted (14, then 7, then 2), three recordings with the same treatment (30, then 16, then 5), a glossary of 40 terms tested three times, and two mock runs counted by two listeners with one tally sheet.

The most useful page for the next candidate is the fault table: it shows which faults were worth a week of work (hesitation, 11 of the 30 counted) and which were small enough to leave until last (the 3 English words, none of them in the final run). It also shows the two faults still in draft 3, found in the last read and corrected in the fair copy printed in this dossier: the counts here are what was found, not what was hoped for.

pages.heading: What this dossier is, and what it is not
pages.body: This is an invented dossier, written for CSEC Compass so that a student can see what a finished written task, a finished talk and an honest reflection look like when they are counted rather than guessed at.
bullets: Invented for this sample: the candidate, the school, the two listeners, the teacher's eight questions, the glossary and every count, score and recording in these pages.

Reused because our guide already publishes them: the investigation topic itself, the opening of the report, and the closing line of the talk, which the candidate kept word for word and then extended into the investigation.

Not to be used as a script. The questions follow the candidate's own research and the answers describe the candidate's own life and work; a recited dossier sounds like a recitation, which is the opposite of what this task is marked on.

The marks columns are the marks our guide lists for each task, 10 of 10 for the written task, 10 of 10 for the oral component and 5 of 5 for the reflection. Our guide publishes no official exam weighting and this sample claims none.
The Spanish in the tables is quoted as it was written and spoken, including the faults counted in it; nothing was tidied after counting.
The copy protection on this card is a nudge to study it, not to paste it: the served file can still be read by anyone who wants to, and no part of it should be submitted as anyone's own work.

examinerNotes: The written task is evidenced by counted drafts rather than by a claim: 667 words over 36 sentences in the finished report, 14, 7 and 2 faults found in the three drafts, and the tense check illustrated with a sentence of the report for each tense it uses.

The glossary is evidenced by three self-tests on the same 40 terms (22, then 31, then 37 correct), with the 3 terms still shaky in week 9 named and the card that settled each of the first test's 18 misses recorded beside it.

The oral component is evidenced by three recordings of the whole six-section talk, with the faults counted down from 30 to 16 to 5 and the two judged runs counted by two listeners from one tally sheet.

The talk is genuinely spoken rather than recited: 127 key words on the cue cards produced 441 words of talk in the final run, 19 of the 40 glossary terms were used in speech, and the eight answers run from four prepared word for word to three improvised on the day.

The reflection is candid and quantified: it keeps the two weeks that lost most of their sessions, the 3 English words that slipped into the first rehearsal and the two faults still in draft 3, which the last read found and the fair copy corrects.

Honesty: this is a sample, not a real submission. The candidate, the school, the two listeners, the eight questions, the glossary and every count are invented for CSEC Compass; the topic and two model lines come from our own guide, and no published material is reproduced.
